problem: Consider a \(10 \times 10\) board where each cell is painted either black or white. A cell is defined as "out of place" if it has at least seven neighbors of a different color. Neighbors include cells that share a side or a corner. Determine the maximum number of white cells on the board that can be "out of place" simultaneously.

answer_text:
# Maximum "Out of Place" White Cells on a 10×10 Board

## Setting Up the Constraints

First, I need to understand which cells can possibly be "out of place" (having ≥ 7 neighbors of a different color):

- **Corner cells:** 3 neighbors → cannot reach 7 → **impossible**
- **Edge cells (non-corner):** 5 neighbors → cannot reach 7 → **impossible**  
- **Interior cells (rows 2–9, cols 2–9):** 8 neighbors → possible (need ≥ 7 different-color neighbors)

So only the **8×8 = 64 interior cells** can be "out of place." For a white interior cell to be "out of place," it needs **at most 1 white neighbor** among its 8 neighbors.

## Upper Bound via 2×2 Block Partition

I partition the 8×8 interior into sixteen disjoint 2×2 blocks:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline B_{1,1} & B_{1,2} & B_{1,3} & B_{1,4} \\
\hline B_{2,1} & B_{2,2} & B_{2,3} & B_{2,4} \\
\hline B_{3,1} & B_{3,2} & B_{3,3} & B_{3,4} \\
\hline B_{4,1} & B_{4,2} & B_{4,3} & B_{4,4} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

**Key observation:** Within any 2×2 block, all four cells are mutually adjacent under 8-connectivity (sharing sides or corners). Therefore:
- If **3 or 4** cells in a block were white, at least one cell would have **≥ 2 white neighbors** within that block alone, violating the "at most 1 white neighbor" constraint.
- So **at most 2 white cells per 2×2 block.**

This gives the upper bound:
$$\text{Max white "out of place" cells} \leq 2 \times 16 = 32$$

## Achievability: The Checkerboard Pattern

Color the board in a standard checkerboard pattern (cell $(i,j)$ is white iff $i+j$ is even).

**Verification for each 2×2 block:** Exactly 2 diagonal cells are white. No two white cells are adjacent (horizontally, vertically, or diagonally).

**Checking the "out of place" condition:** Every white interior cell has all 8 neighbors black (since no white cell is adjacent to any other white cell). Thus each white interior cell has 8 black neighbors ≥ 7. ✓

**Counting:** The 8×8 interior contains exactly 32 white cells (one per 2×2 block diagonal × 16 blocks), and **all 32 are "out of place."**

Edge cells are colored alternately but cannot be "out of place" regardless (they have < 7 neighbors), so they don't affect the count.

## Conclusion

The upper bound of 32 is tight, achieved by the checkerboard coloring.

$$\boxed{32}$$
